source.title: What Is a Repeated Token Worth? The Scaling Geometry of Multi-Epoch Pretraining

page_placements.theme: Repeated data, finite data and stopping have capacity-dependent value

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures scaling under repeated-data pretraining and argues that repetition costs depend on the baseline, what is held fixed, and how data are repeated; it also reports settings where fitted loss surfaces fail.
record.gate_note: The paper measures held-out loss and scaling outcomes for repeated-data runs. It also discusses prior studies, but cited results are not recorded as rows. Values used only to select fits or recipes are not rows. The paper's main findings about the cost of repetition, fixed-data allocation, and sensitivity to repetition layout are included.
record.test_reason: The study fits and checks power laws for repeated-data pretraining loss on text (V5). It shows that the excess-loss exponent, the size term and the size trend change with parameter counting, partial versus full repetition, what is held fixed and the fitting form (V7). It derives a compute-optimal N/epoch split at fixed unique data (V3, data-constrained setting) and checks a fitted surface on held-out 1B/2B models (V2, modest extrapolation). Several of its claims argue that published repetition laws need restating, hence T5.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that against fresh data at equal compute, repetition cost follows z=(R−1)Ntotal/U. Together with the one-epoch curve, z explains the critical epoch count, the fixed-U split (size and epochs grow roughly as √C until loss stops improving near Rc), and the direction of size trends under each design. Order, allocation, source entropy and tokenization also change loss at identical counts. They add that scaling studies should report the baseline and the quantity held fixed.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses new repeated-data sweeps and fitted loss comparisons rather than reproducing either original scaling-law recipe. It trains small decoder-only Transformers on SlimPajama with Muon and Adam; the paper notes that its main runs use no weight decay or dropout.
record.method_sensitivity: The measured outcome varies with what is held fixed and which baseline is used, whether embeddings are included in parameter count, full versus partial repetition, repeated fraction, sample concentration, shard order, source entropy, tokenizer schedule, optimizer, and the unique-data range used for a fit.

fits_no_version.finding: A second repeated epoch is worth 0.87–1.02 of a fresh token; value falls with epochs and rises with tokens per parameter.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Early repeated epochs are nearly as valuable as fresh data, with value decaying with R and recovering with D/N.

fits_no_version.finding: BPE-dropout raises loss at R≤4 and lowers it at R≥8 (−0.154 bpb at R=16).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Stochastic re-tokenization reduces the cost of heavy data reuse but hurts at low reuse.

fits_no_version.finding: At R=32, Muon degrades more than AdamW relative to its own one-epoch loss (0.755 vs 0.608 bpb).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimizer choice changes the magnitude of multi-epoch degradation.

record.problems: Models are much smaller than frontier systems. Many grid and sweep configurations have one replicate; paired studies generally use three replicates. The 0.002-bpb resolution threshold limits interpretation of small differences, and some fitted surfaces are inaccurate outside their fit range. The study uses recipes without weight decay or dropout and does not evaluate downstream capabilities.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows omitted under the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: The general power law in N, D or C over several orders of magnitude is not tested. A one-epoch Chinchilla backbone (23M–361M) is fitted only as a tool.
Prediction of runs orders of magnitude larger is not tested. The held-out check reaches only 2–4× beyond the largest fitted size (511M to 1B/2B).
The compute-optimal split with fresh, unconstrained data is not tested. With fixed U, the allocation is mostly fitted; only approximate IsoFLOP bins at U=1B are measured.
There is no depth/width variation at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities, fine-tuning and transfer are not tested; only repeated-data text pretraining.
Training-schedule effects on fitted exponents and a comparison of fresh-data Kaplan vs Chinchilla splits are not tested.

missing.what: In the mixed-corpus fixed-budget sweep, Eq. (3) with a size factor fits p=0.88 and g=0.46, against the grid's p=1.07 and g=−0.02. Exponent and size dependence change with setup.
The joint additive fit gives exponent p'=1.25, against p=1.07 from the excess-loss fit on the same grid.
Approximate IsoFLOP minima at U=1B give N* ∝ C^0.70 (six minima) and C^1.0 (R=4 minima), and the count-based surface gives 0.87/0.93. The fitted frontier gives 0.52–0.53.
The one-epoch Chinchilla backbone fitted to 35 fresh runs (23M–361M, D/N 0.3–300) gives E=0.583, α=0.305, β=0.188 with RMSE 0.86%. Its fresh-data optimum is TPP≈25.
The penalty-form choice changes held-out-size prediction: MAE is 0.114 (separable) vs 0.031 (load-augmented) vs 0.088 (benefit-only).
Rc from the one-epoch fit plus Eq. (3) has slope 0.31 against the measured 0.24. Its crossings lie 27–34% below the measured ones at TPP 5.

record.verdict_notes: Models are 14M–2B with no weight decay or dropout, and many sweeps are single-replicate. The V3 evidence is in a data-constrained regime and is mostly from a fitted surface. The fixed-U epoch-minimum rows were re-linked from V3 to V7 because they are per-model optima, not compute-optimal allocations. The low-U surface failures (r29–r32) are extrapolations to smaller unique budgets, so they bear on V7, not V2. Neither original source is this study.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test the general held-out loss power laws in parameter count, tokens, or compute when the other quantities are not bottlenecks. Its repetition-cost power law is a different quantity.

The paper checks a fitted repetition-loss surface on larger model sizes and on unique-data budgets below its fit range, but does not test predictions for runs orders of magnitude larger in the general pretraining-loss setting.

The compute-optimal frontier is studied with unique data fixed, and its model-size and epoch exponents are reported. The paper does not test the general compute-optimal split when data are fresh and unconstrained.
No controlled test of depth, width, or architecture variation at fixed parameter count.
The study tests repeated-data pretraining on text. It does not test other modalities, fine-tuning, or transfer.
The study reports held-out loss, not downstream-task performance.
The study tests setup and fitting sensitivity for repeated-data scaling, not the full range of setup choices in the original scaling-law studies.
